title: Quantum Simulation of Markovian and Non-Markovian Open Quantum Dynamics in Heavy-Ion Collisions
abstract: We present a quantum computing framework for simulating open-quantum-system approaches based on Markovian and non-Markovian dynamics, which is relevant to heavy-ion collisions. To simulate the non-Markovian evolution on quantum computers, we introduce an auxiliary two-level pseudomode that carries the memory forward and couples to both the subsystem and the residual Markovian bath. We explicitly show that tracing out the pseudomode reproduces the non-Markovian evolution with the exact memory kernel. Moreover, in the relevant time scale hierarchy, the quantum circuit construction of the pseudomode smoothly converges to the Markovian limit. For a given bath memory kernel, our results demonstrate the feasibility of quantum simulations of both Markovian and non-Markovian dynamics, establishing a framework for future studies of hard probes such as jets, heavy quarks, and quarkonia in heavy-ion collisions.
summary: This paper develops a quantum computing framework to simulate open quantum dynamics relevant to heavy-ion collisions, covering both Markovian and non-Markovian regimes. It achieves this by introducing an auxiliary pseudomode that explicitly carries the bath's memory, allowing for accurate simulation of complex time evolution. The framework validates the feasibility of using quantum circuits for studying hard probes in extreme physical environments.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of simulating open quantum system dynamics, specifically modeling the interaction of a subsystem with a thermal bath in the context of heavy-ion collisions.
main_result: A quantum computing framework is established that successfully simulates both Markovian and non-Markovian open quantum evolution by introducing an auxiliary pseudomode to capture memory effects.
method: The simulation employs a quantum circuit approach, utilizing an auxiliary two-level pseudomode to model the bath memory kernel, which is then traced out to recover the full non-Markovian dynamics.
model_or_system: The system models a subsystem (e.g., a bound state) interacting with a thermal bath, described by a general non-Markovian master equation. The dynamics are analyzed in the non-relativistic effective field theory framework.
key_observables: Survival probability of the bound state ($P_{bound}(t)$), and the reduced subsystem density matrix ($ho_S$).
important_parameters: Bath correlation time ($	au_c$), which dictates the transition between the Markovian ($	au_c 	o 0$) and non-Markovian ($	au_c \sim 1/E_b$) regimes.
main_assumptions: The bath is assumed stationary, and the analysis relies on introducing a pseudomode to explicitly handle the memory kernel, which is shown to converge to the Markovian limit when appropriate time scales are considered.

paper_structure: The paper first establishes the general non-Markovian master equation, then introduces the pseudomode technique to model memory effects, derives the Markovian limit (Lindblad form), and finally demonstrates the feasibility of simulating both regimes using quantum circuits.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it provides a concrete, implementable quantum simulation protocol for complex, memory-dependent open quantum dynamics, bridging theoretical physics with quantum computation.

The ancillas are traced out TrE[·] and re-prepared fresh before the next repetition. Iterating this single unitary Nstep times describes the evolution of Eq. (8) over total time t = Nstep∆t.

FIG. 3. Circuit realization of two non-Markovian time steps. The subsystem qubit |ψS⟩and pseudomode qubit |ψP ⟩ (dashed line) both persist across repetitions and are never reset. Each step applies the symmetric splitting: a coher- ent half-step USP (∆t/2) acting on the subsystem and pseu- domode; the dissipative step Upm(∆t) acting on the pseudo- mode and a fresh environment ancilla |ψE⟩, which is traced out immediately afterward; and a second coherent half-step USP (∆t/2) on the subsystem and pseudomode. Repeating this three-unitary sequence Nstep times describes the evolu- tion over total time t = Nstep∆t.
